questions.prompt: What is __name__ when you run a file directly?
questions.explain: Python sets __name__ to "__main__" in whichever file it was told to run. That is the fact the whole pattern is built on.

questions.prompt: What is __name__ inside greetings.py when another file does `import greetings`?
questions.explain: An imported module gets its own module name. That is how the guard can tell the two situations apart.

questions.prompt: Put these lines in the order a module with a self-test uses.
questions.explain: The definitions come first so that both a direct run and an import get them, and the test sits at the bottom behind the guard.

questions.prompt: Which of these are true of code placed inside `if __name__ == "__main__":`?
choices: It runs when the file is run directly
It is skipped when the file is imported
It is a good place for demo and test code
It makes the functions above it private
questions.explain: The guard only controls when that block runs. The functions above stay perfectly importable, which is the point.
